description.narrative: Tujifunze Tujilinde Project is a youth-led Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights initiative implemented by TAMSA–MUHAS in Tanzania’s Pwani Region. It addresses the lack of accurate, youth-friendly SRHR information among adolescents covering puberty,menstrual hygiene, and consequences of early pregnancy which often leads to misinformation, stigma, teenage pregnancy, and HIV/STIs. Building on prior outreach that reached 928 students in Kisarawe, the project innovates by combining peer-led school sessions with a permanent, youth-designed comic handbook for ongoing reference. It aims to directly educate 5,000 students across four schools, train peer educators, build comic design skills for sustainability, and support learning with demonstration kits andsocial media campaigns. The project aims to extend SRHR education beyond one-time sessions, fostering informed choices, reducing stigma, and strengthening youth-led health advocacy through sustainable,student-centered methods. The goal is to create a sustainable improvement in adolescent SRHR knowledge and attitudes in Pwani Region. The main objective is to strengthen this knowledge through a combined model of interactive school outreach and the distribution of a student-centered handbook. Key activities include: designing, and printing 2500 copies of an innovative SRHR comic handbook, conducting peer-facilitated outreach sessions in 4 secondary schools, training student medical volunteers to provide clear information during outreaches, training selected medical students to design comics for sustainability, forming adolescent school health clubs,and social media campaign to amplify the handbook's content.

participating-org.narrative:
TAMSA is Tanzania’s national, youth-led organization representing medical students. It evolved from the Dar es Salaam Medical Students Association (1968) into a formal association in the 1990s, uniting students to advance medical training, leadership, and community health.
TAMSA operates through university chapters, such as TAMSA–MUHAS at Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences, which advocates for students' academic, professional, and social welfare while fostering collaboration with university leadership on education quality and student well-being.
Guided by a mission to equip students with skills to tackle community health challenges through evidence-based and rights-focused approaches, TAMSA runs programs via specialized committees: Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SCORA), public health, research, social affairs, and student exchange—all with an intersectional health lens.
The association promotes healthy practices nationwide through medical camps, health education talk shows, online outreach, and community initiatives. Upholding values of youth leadership, professionalism, and service, TAMSA envisions empowering future physicians to improvehealth outcomes in Tanzania and beyond.
TAMSA–MUHAS exemplifies this mission by mobilizing students for health promotion activities including medical camps, webinars, research workshops, and campaigns such as "Rejesha Tabasamu" (menstrual health campaign) and Afya Fiesta (NCDs awareness campaign) directly benefiting Tanzanian communities.
